risks.note: Management's first-named risk in both the MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' and 'Threats' lists: fluctuations in the prices and availability of key raw materials may impact production costs and profitability. Structurally acute for a ferrous foundry, whose input cost is dominated by pig iron, scrap and melt fuel; the industry commentary the Company itself reproduces notes coke import quota cuts driving delivered prices from about USD 360 to nearly USD 480 per tonne and squeezing foundry margins by 4-6 points.

Management flags that changes in demand, production schedules or procurement strategies of key OEM customers may impact business performance. On a company of this size (118 permanent employees as at 31 March 2026, a single foundry site), the loss or de-stocking of one anchor OEM would be material; the AR does not disclose the actual concentration percentage or a named customer list, so the magnitude cannot be quantified from this report.
risks.risk: Customer concentration in a small OEM base

risks.note: Explicitly named by management: efficient ramp-up and optimum utilisation of the newly commissioned manufacturing facility remain important for achieving the expected operational and financial benefits. The new 12,000 MTPA line started only on 2 March 2026 and more than doubles installed capacity to 19,200 MTPA, while Unit 1 itself ran at only 76.20% utilisation. Fixed cost and depreciation land immediately; volume must be found to absorb them.
risks.risk: Ramp-up and utilisation risk on the newly commissioned Unit 2

risks.note: Demand from automobile, railway, engineering and industrial machinery end-markets is influenced by overall economic conditions and industry cycles. Castings sit early in the OEM supply chain, so an OEM slowdown transmits to the Company amplified through the order book and through the destocking cycle.

Management names a competitive market that may exert pressure on pricing and margins. The Indian foundry sector is highly fragmented with a large micro-foundry tail, while the industry commentary the Company cites names much larger competitors (Brakes India, JSW Steel, Larsen & Toubro, Kirloskar Ferrous, Bharat Forge). A sub-20,000 MTPA foundry has limited pricing power against OEM buyers.
risks.risk: Intense competition compressing pricing and margins

risks.note: Changes in environmental, labour, taxation and other statutory regulations may increase compliance requirements and require operational adjustments. Foundries are energy- and emission-intensive; the Company's own cited industry text discusses tightening sulfur caps on imported coke and hydrogen-furnace conversion pressure, either of which would raise the compliance cost base.
risks.risk: Regulatory and compliance risk, particularly environmental

risks.note: Management states that continuous investments in automation, process improvements and quality systems are essential to meet evolving customer requirements and maintain competitiveness. This is a durable capital-intensity risk: RDSO Class 'A' and automotive quality accreditations must be maintained to retain railway and OEM approvals, so reinvestment is not discretionary.
risks.risk: Technology and quality-expectation risk requiring continuous reinvestment

risks.note: The debt-equity ratio rose to 0.38 from 0.11 because of higher borrowings availed during the year to support the commissioning of the new automated facility and capacity expansion. Absolute leverage remains modest, but the step-up means the ramp-up risk on Unit 2 now carries a financing obligation alongside it.
risks.risk: Increased leverage taken on to fund the expansion

currentContext.expansion: The defining expansion event of FY2025-26 was the commissioning of a new automated manufacturing facility (Unit 2) at Kashipur, Uttarakhand. The new facility adds 12,000 MTPA of installed capacity on top of the existing Unit 1 capacity of 7,200 MTPA, taking total installed capacity to 19,200 MTPA - an increase of 166.67%. Trial and commercial operations of the new facility commenced with effect from 2 March 2026, so it contributed to only the last month of FY2025-26. The capacity expansion is stated to be in line with the objects of the IPO, particularly the capital expenditure earmarked for acquisition of plant and machinery; the Company completed its IPO and listed on the BSE SME Platform on 6 October 2025, allotting 49,70,000 equity shares of face value Rs 10 at a premium of Rs 46 per share. Management describes the facility as equipped with advanced manufacturing technologies and automation, enhancing productivity, process consistency and scalability. Unit 1 operated at 76.20% capacity utilisation (actual production 5,487 MTPA against 7,200 MTPA installed) during the year. The forward plan is a ramp of the new facility rather than a further announced project: no new capex project, no rupee capex budget, and no further capacity addition is announced in this annual report. Management explicitly flags that efficient ramp-up and optimum utilisation of the newly commissioned facility remain important for realising the expected operational and financial benefits, and that higher borrowings availed to support the commissioning lifted the debt-equity ratio during the year. The Company had no subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures during the year, so no inorganic capacity addition is disclosed.

This is a durable capital-intensity risk: RDSO Class 'A' and automotive quality accreditations must be maintained to retain railway and OEM approvals, so reinvestment is not discretionary.

risks.risk: Increased leverage taken on to fund the expansion
risks.note: The debt-equity ratio rose to 0.38 from 0.11 because of higher borrowings availed during the year to support the commissioning of the new automated facility and capacity expansion. Absolute leverage remains modest, but the step-up means the ramp-up risk on Unit 2 now carries a financing obligation alongside it.

Both manufacturing units are at the same Kashipur, Uttarakhand location and the Company reports a single line of business (castings) with no subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures. Any site-level disruption - power, environmental clearance, labour or natural event - would affect the whole of production. This is a structural concentration read off the plant and entity disclosures rather than a risk the Company labels as such.

business_model.title: Business (RHP)
business_model.body: The Company manufactures and sells CI castings, SG Iron castings, High Carbon Steel castings, Gun Metal castings, Brass castings and other metal products for engineering applications. It supplies precision-engineered castings - engine, transmission, braking, steering, chassis and cooling components - to OEMs and industrial customers across the automobile, railway, agricultural machinery, heavy engineering, sugar and energy & power generation industries. capex_expansion.title: Expansion (RHP)
capex_expansion.body: The defining expansion event of FY2025-26 was the commissioning of a new automated manufacturing facility (Unit 2) at Kashipur, Uttarakhand. The new facility adds 12,000 MTPA of installed capacity on top of the existing Unit 1 capacity of 7,200 MTPA, taking total installed capacity to 19,200 MTPA - an increase of 166.67%. Trial and commercial operations of the new facility commenced with effect from 2 March 2026, so it contributed to only the last month of FY2025-26. risks.title: Risks (RHP)
risks.body:
- Management's first-named risk in both the MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' and 'Threats' lists: fluctuations in the prices and availability of key raw materials may impact production costs and profitability. Structurally acute for a ferrous foundry, whose input cost is dominated by pig iron, scrap and melt fuel; the industry commentary the Company itself reproduces notes coke import quota cuts driving delivered prices from about USD 360 to nearly USD 480 per tonne and squeezing foundry margins by 4-6 points.
- Management flags that changes in demand, production schedules or procurement strategies of key OEM customers may impact business performance. On a company of this size (118 permanent employees as at 31 March 2026, a single foundry site), the loss or de-stocking of one anchor OEM would be material; the AR does not disclose the actual concentration percentage or a named customer list, so the magnitude cannot be quantified from this report.
- Explicitly named by management: efficient ramp-up and optimum utilisation of the newly commissioned manufacturing facility remain important for achieving the expected operational and financial benefits. The new 12,000 MTPA line started only on 2 March 2026 and more than doubles installed capacity to 19,200 MTPA, while Unit 1 itself ran at only 76.20% utilisation. Fixed cost and depreciation land immediately; volume must be found to absorb them.
- Demand from automobile, railway, engineering and industrial machinery end-markets is influenced by overall economic conditions and industry cycles. Castings sit early in the OEM supply chain, so an OEM slowdown transmits to the Company amplified through the order book and through the destocking cycle.
- Management names a competitive market that may exert pressure on pricing and margins. The Indian foundry sector is highly fragmented with a large micro-foundry tail, while the industry commentary the Company cites names much larger competitors (Brakes India, JSW Steel, Larsen & Toubro, Kirloskar Ferrous, Bharat Forge). A sub-20,000 MTPA foundry has limited pricing power against OEM buyers.
- Changes in environmental, labour, taxation and other statutory regulations may increase compliance requirements and require operational adjustments. Foundries are energy- and emission-intensive; the Company's own cited industry text discusses tightening sulfur caps on imported coke and hydrogen-furnace conversion pressure, either of which would raise the compliance cost base.
- Management states that continuous investments in automation, process improvements and quality systems are essential to meet evolving customer requirements and maintain competitiveness. This is a durable capital-intensity risk: RDSO Class 'A' and automotive quality accreditations must be maintained to retain railway and OEM approvals, so reinvestment is not discretionary.
- The debt-equity ratio rose to 0.38 from 0.11 because of higher borrowings availed during the year to support the commissioning of the new automated facility and capacity expansion. Absolute leverage remains modest, but the step-up means the ramp-up risk on Unit 2 now carries a financing obligation alongside it.
